landing.title: Threshold
landing.tagline: An agent that knows exactly when to stop and ask.
landing.persona: Built for Priya Nakamura's team — the 22 examiners in Fenwick Mutual's Property Claims Payments unit, who lose a third of every claim's cycle time bouncing between systems for routine lookups, and need a hard guarantee that no payout above a threshold can ever bypass a supervisor's review.
landing.feature1.title: Real Human-in-the-Loop
landing.feature1.body: A payout above threshold genuinely pauses execution and waits for a real approval — the one guardrail a typical first-pass build never actually wires in.
landing.feature2.title: Amount-aware approval
landing.feature2.body: Small payouts flow straight through; only payouts over an admin-set threshold ever need a human — not every payout, unconditionally.
landing.feature3.title: A corrected safety order
landing.feature3.body: Step limit, then permission, then cost cap, then human approval — in that exact order, with the reasoning made visible, not just implemented.
landing.feature4.title: A tamper-evident audit trail
landing.feature4.body: Every AI call and every guardrail decision is hash-chained — an admin can verify the log hasn't been altered after the fact.
landing.disclaimer: Fenwick Mutual is a fictional company created for this project. Threshold is a demo — payout amounts and thresholds are illustrative only and do not represent real financial transactions.

admin.guardrailOrderNote: Why permission is checked before cost cap: a common bug in naive implementations of this pattern checks these in the wrong order, mislabeling an unauthorized-tool attempt as a budget event instead of a permission violation once the budget happens to already be exhausted. Threshold checks step limit, then permission, then cost cap, then human approval — always in that order.
